messages.subject: debug by print; constrained parameters
parts:
I'm taking the response (inline) back to the list.

On 2/20/13 9:40 AM, M.F. Jonker wrote:
> Hi Bob,
>
> It definitely takes time to get used to the ordering of statements!

Stan works like other programming languages.
It took me a while to get used to the fact that BUGS wasn't
ordered.

> But when I make an error in the execution order, I
> could previously observe what went wrong via print()-statements. For example, using print I learned that this is
> required in STAN:
> /for (a in 1:A){
> lambda[a] <- exp( ... ) ;
> }
> for (a in 1:A){
> prob[a] <- lambda[a] / (lambda[1] + lambda[2]) ;
> }/
>
> whereas this is sufficient for BUGS:
> /for (a in 1:A){
> lambda[a] <- exp( ... ) ;
> prob[a] <- lambda[a] / (lambda[1] + lambda[2]) ;
> }
>
> /However, this time the error is thrown even before my print statements are executed (and thus before the likelihood
> with undefined variables could have been problematic). How do I debug errors in this case?

You can drop in prints and then the error's right after
the first print that breaks.

You can print parameters in the transformed parameters block
or at the top of the model.

> I also implemented your suggestions in the code (didn't know that sqrt(X)would be faster than pow(X,0.5)after
> compilation)

Actually -- it probably won't. I think I modified
pow(x,0.5) to call sqrt(x) -- so the only overhead is
a pretty-fast branch, not an inefficient call to pow or
a too-general derivative.

> but I did not understand why and how I could ensure proper boundaries on mu_s. It is an implied value that
> depends on sigma_s; the latter is constrained to be positive, which effectively constrains mu_s as well (I would say?).

The issue here is a part of a model the user doesn't want to
share, the important point of which is this:

parameters {
...
vector[N] s_star;
...
model {
...
s_star[n] ~ lognormal(mu_s , sigma_s) T[0.015,10];
...

You want to declare s_star with the appropriate constraint, or Stan
will get stuck if any of the s_star[n] ever wanders outside of
its support. The declaration should be:

parameters {
vector<lower=0.015,upper=10>[N] s_star;
...

- Bob

But also Y ~ Poisson( prob ) results in a parsing error.

for (a in 1:A){

sum[n,t,a] <- alpha[a] + s[n] * dot_product(X[n,t,a], beta[n]);

parts:
On 2/20/13 3:29 PM, Marcel Jonker wrote:
> Hi Bob,
>
> Thank you very much (!) Learning a lot about STAN here :)
> As a next step, what would be the best strategy to vectorize the for-loops in the likelihood? N is by far the largest
> dimension, but I had trouble assigning a multivariate normal on each slice of a matrix beta[N,V] (probably just my
> mistake). But also Y ~ Poisson( prob ) results in a parsing error.
>
> ## N = 1500
> ## T = 14
> ## A = 2
> ## V = 22
>
> ## vector[V] beta[N];
> ## vector[V] X[N,T,A];
>
> for (n in 1:N){
> for (t in 1:T){
> for (a in 1:A){
> sum[n,t,a] <- alpha[a] + s[n] * dot_product(X[n,t,a], beta[n]);
> # truncate to avoid numerical overflows
> if (sum[n,t,a] < -250)
> sum[n,t,a] <- -250;
> else if (sum[n,t,a] > 250)
> sum[n,t,a] <- 250;
> lambda[n,t,a] <- exp(sum[n,t,a]) ;
> }
> for (a in 1:A){
> prob[n,t,a] <- lambda[n,t,a] / (lambda[n,t,1] + lambda[n,t,2]) ;
> Y[n, t, a] ~ poisson( prob[n,t,a] ) ;
> }}}

Is A = 2?

The problem with truncating these sums like this is that it
breaks the connection to auto-diff. This is not a good thing
for Stan, because as soon as the sums overflow, we lose any
gradient information. I don't know enough about your model to see
how to do this differently. Maybe with some other kind of transform?
Or with constraints on beta derived from the data?c

If you declare things as vectors, you can vectorize the sum calc.

For the Poisson, you should be able to use this:
for (a in 1:A)

Y[n,t] ~ poisson(lambda[n,t] / (lambda[n,t,1] - lambda[n,t,2]);

It's most efficient in this case to define Y by:

real Y[N,T,A];

or

vector[A] Y[N,T];

That will cut out internal copies.

I'd stick to standard styles, too -- the pileup of "}}}" is going to be
hard for anyone to scan who's used to standard programming languages.

> # priors
> for (n in 1:N){
> beta[n] ~ multi_normal(mu_beta, sigma) ;
> s[n] ~ lognormal(mu_s , sigma_s) T[0.015,10];
> }

I'm not sure where we're at on this, but the multi_normal hasn't
been fully vetorized yet.

And we haven't vectorized truncated distributions.

The above is what requires s to be declared with upper and lower
bounds.

- Bob

At first, I thought it was because I incorrectly specified the respondent-specific scaling terms (which are given a lognormal prior); hence my question about how to sample from a prior in STAN. I attached the model file and sample dataset; the model is compiled with option -O0 and I initialized the runs with --init=0 to avoid the previous run-time errors.

Best,
Marcel
